title: Dental Office Photography: Your Web Profile Matters to Patients
summary: Dental office photography for DSOs and growing practices: what to shoot, how to schedule around patients, and where the photos earn new patients.
body_markdown:
## The photos your patients care about


Before a new patient books a cleaning, they've usually seen your practice on a phone screen. The map pin. The directory profile. The website's "Meet the team" page. If those images are a blurry exterior from 2017 and a stock photo of a smiling model, the practice down the road with real photos of its real team has the edge.


Tebra's 2025 patient survey of nearly 4,000 people found that 79% of patients read reviews before they choose a provider, and 56% start their research on Google.


We spoke with the marketing lead at a dental support organization that supports around 100 offices in several states, from rural towns to big metros. Since they started working with Snappr, the team has scheduled more than 30 office shoots. Here's the playbook they've built.


The waiting area is often the first photo patients see, on maps and directory profiles.


## What to shoot at a dental office


The group's brief is an itemized list so standard that the marketing lead describes reusing it as "copy, paste, copy, paste." For a typical office, it covers:


1. Exterior with signage, shot straight on, so patients recognize the building when they arrive.


2. Reception and waiting area, wide and well lit.


3. One or two operatories, clean and prepared as if for a patient.


4. Any technology worth showing: imaging, scanners, a sterilization area.


5. A full team photo, usually 5 to 10 people: dentists, hygienists, assistants, office manager and front desk.


6. Individual portraits for every dentist and hygienist. Our guide to[doctor headshots](https://www.snappr.com/blog/doctor-headshots) covers wardrobe and setup.


Groups like this are a growing share of dentistry. The ADA Health Policy Institute reports that about one in six US dentists (17%) were affiliated with a dental support organization as of 2025, and every new office that joins a group needs photos that match the rest.


## Schedule around patients, not against them


Getting 5 to 10 clinical staff free at the same time is the hardest part of any dental shoot. The group handles it centrally: the marketing team agrees a date with each office manager, books the photographer, and sends a calendar invite so the whole office knows when to be camera-ready.


A few tips from their process:


• Book the first hour of the day or a blocked lunch, before or between patients.


• Make the office manager the on-site contact. They know which rooms are free.


• Send the shot list ahead so the team knows what to wear and which rooms to prepare.


If team photos are new for your offices, our piece on[why team photos shape how a company is seen](https://www.snappr.com/blog/why-your-startups-team-photos-can-make-or-break-your-company-image) makes the case to skeptical staff.


Show the care, not just the chairs. Real clinicians at work beat a stock smile.


## Put one shoot to work in five places


This group doesn't shoot for the website alone. Every gallery is split across several channels:


• The practice website, through their web vendor.


• Google Maps listings.


• Zocdoc and OpenCare profiles.


• Next on the list: Yelp, Healthgrades and paid search.


Directories carry real weight with patients. rater8's 2026 Patient Choice Report found that review sites such as Healthgrades, Vitals and WebMD most influenced the choice of doctor for 40% of patients surveyed. Google's Business Profile help center adds that customers are 2.7 times more likely to consider a business reputable when they find a complete Business Profile on Search and Maps.


Plan crops for each channel before you shoot. Directory thumbnails are small and square, so a clean exterior and a tight team photo do better there than a wide room shot.


## From one office to a hundred


The group's marketing lead summed up why they work this way: before a vendor like Snappr, "these types of services didn't exist to be able to scale photos quickly." Bringing offices into a group gives each one access to tools a single practice would rarely set up, which the marketing lead calls a "compounding effect of efficiency."

## Frequently asked questions


### What photos should a dental office have on its website?


Most dental websites need an exterior with signage, the reception area, at least one treatment room, a team photo and individual portraits of each dentist and hygienist. Real photos of your own office and team build more trust than stock images.


### How long does a dental office photoshoot take?


A single-office shoot covering the space, a team photo and individual portraits usually fits into one to two hours. Booking early in the day or over a blocked lunch keeps it from interrupting patients.


### Can a dental group use the same photographer brief for every office?


Yes. Groups with many offices get the most consistent results from one standard shot list sent to every photographer, with the office manager as the on-site contact for each shoot.
